title: Right Triangle Trigonometry with SOHCAHTOA
description: Sketch and label SAT right triangles, choose and solve exact sine, cosine, and tangent equations, manage degree and radian mode, and transfer trig ratios across similar triangles.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first idea, even if you are unsure. You can continue without submitting an answer.

shared_prompt.title: Similar triangles JKL and MNP
shared_prompt.html:
Right triangles \(JKL\) and \(MNP\) are similar, with \(J\leftrightarrow M\), \(K\leftrightarrow N\), and \(L\leftrightarrow P\). Angles \(L\) and \(P\) are right angles. Also, \(\angle J=52^\circ\), \(JL=7\), and \(MP=20\).

Which is the exact length of \(NP\)?

  1. \(7\tan(52^\circ)\)
  2. \(\dfrac{20}{\tan(52^\circ)}\)
  3. \(20\cos(52^\circ)\)
  4. \(20\tan(52^\circ)\)

figure.alt: Two similar right triangles are shown separately, not to scale. JKL is right at L, angle J is 52 degrees, and JL is 7. MNP is right at P, angle M is marked, MP is 20, and NP is unknown.
figure.caption: Diagrams not drawn to scale. Use the given correspondence J ↔ M.

blocks.html:
Turn the triangle into a side ratio

The opening question has point labels and an angle, but the needed length is not obvious. Trigonometry connects an acute angle in a right triangle to ratios of its sides.

We’ll start by naming the sides from one marked angle, then choose a ratio and use it to find a length.

Find the right angle and chosen angle

Find the side across from the right angle first. Then look from angle B to name the other two sides.

content.prompt: Which description always identifies the hypotenuse of a right triangle?
choices: The side directly below the marked acute angle
The shortest side in the drawing
The side opposite whichever angle is labeled \(\theta\)
content.hint: The hypotenuse is defined using the right angle, not the location or rotation of the drawing.
content.explanation: The hypotenuse is always across from the \(90^\circ\) angle, and it is the triangle's longest side.

blocks.html:
Name the sides from the angle you use

  • Hypotenuse: across from 90°.
  • Opposite: across from the chosen acute angle.
  • Adjacent: the other leg touching that angle.

Changing the acute angle swaps opposite and adjacent. The hypotenuse stays the same.

figure.alt: Triangle ABC is right at C, with the chosen angle at B: AC is opposite, BC is adjacent, and AB is the hypotenuse.
figure.caption: Changing the chosen acute angle swaps opposite and adjacent.

content.prompt: A right triangle's two legs are \(AB\) and \(BC\), and its hypotenuse is \(AC\). Relative to acute angle \(A\), which side is opposite?
content.hint: The opposite side does not touch angle A.
content.explanation: Side \(BC\) sits across from angle \(A\). Side \(AB\) is adjacent, and \(AC\) is the hypotenuse.

figure.alt: Triangle ABC is right at B; angle A is marked, and all three vertices are labeled. No side is labeled with its trig role.

blocks.html:
Choose among three ratios

SOHCAHTOA is a reminder for:

  • SOH: sine = opposite/hypotenuse.
  • CAH: cosine = adjacent/hypotenuse.
  • TOA: tangent = opposite/adjacent.

Use the ratio containing the known side and requested side.

content.prompt: In right triangle \(PQR\), \(\angle Q=90^\circ\), and the angle being used is \(\angle R\). The question gives \(QR\) and asks for \(PQ\). Which trig function should you use?
content.hint: On your sketch, \(PQ\) is opposite angle R and \(QR\) is adjacent.
content.explanation: The point labels translate to opposite and adjacent, so TOA gives \(\tan(R)=PQ/QR\).

figure.alt: Triangle PQR is right at Q, angle R is marked, side QR is labeled given, and side PQ is labeled with a question mark.

blocks.html:
Sketch, Label, Ratio

  1. Sketch and place the named vertices and angles.
  2. Label opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse from the chosen acute angle.
  3. Choose the ratio using the known and requested sides.
  4. Solve for the requested side.

Keep an exact trig expression when the choices use one.

Match the angle unit before calculating

For a degree angle such as 35°, select Degrees under Graph Settings → Angle Measure before typing tan(35). For radians, select Radians.

The setting tells Desmos how to interpret the angle you type.

content.prompt: A triangle labels an acute angle as \(35^\circ\). What should you do before typing \(\tan(35)\) in Desmos?
choices: Open Graph Settings and select Degrees
Leave Desmos in its default Radians mode
content.hint: The degree symbol tells you how Desmos must interpret 35.
content.explanation: Select Degrees so Desmos treats 35 as \(35^\circ\), not 35 radians.

blocks.html:
Use opposite and adjacent

From angle A, BC=x is opposite and AC=12 is adjacent. So \(\tan35^\circ=x/12\), giving \(x=12\tan35^\circ\). That expression is the exact length.

figure.alt: Triangle ABC is right at C, angle A is 35 degrees, AC is 12, and BC is x.
figure.caption: Read the sides from angle A.

content.prompt: Which equation is correct for triangle ABC?
content.hint: Sketch the triangle. From angle A, BC is opposite and AC is adjacent.
content.explanation: The point labels become opposite \(BC=x\) over adjacent \(AC=12\).

figure.alt: Triangle ABC is right at C, angle A is 35 degrees, AC is 12, and BC is x.
figure.caption: Read the sides from angle A.

blocks.html:
The unknown can be in the denominator

From angle X, YZ=9 is opposite and XZ=h is the hypotenuse. Thus \(\sin28^\circ=9/h\). Solve to get \(h=9/\sin28^\circ\).

figure.alt: Triangle XYZ is right at Y, angle X is 28 degrees, YZ is 9, and XZ is h.
figure.caption: Read the sides from angle X.

content.prompt: Which is the exact value of \(XZ\)?
content.solution:
Start from the equation for this triangle: \(XZ=h\) is the hypotenuse and \(YZ=9\) is opposite \(\angle X\), so \(\sin(28^\circ)=\frac{9}{h}\).
The unknown begins in the denominator, so multiply both sides by \(h\): \(h\sin(28^\circ)=9\).
Divide both sides by \(\sin(28^\circ)\): \(h=\frac{9}{\sin(28^\circ)}\).
Keep it exact rather than converting to a decimal.
So the answer is choice A, \(\frac{9}{\sin(28^\circ)}\).
content.hint: Label the sides from the \(28^\circ\) angle: which role does the given \(9\) play, and which does the unknown play? Set up that ratio and watch where the unknown starts.
content.explanation: Multiplying by h and dividing by \(\sin(28^\circ)\) gives \(XZ=9/\sin(28^\circ)\).

figure.alt: Triangle XYZ is right at Y, angle X is 28 degrees, YZ is 9, and XZ is h.
figure.caption: Read the sides from angle X.

blocks.html:
Adjacent and hypotenuse use cosine

From angle P, PQ=a is adjacent and PR=18 is the hypotenuse. Use \(\cos41^\circ=a/18\), giving \(a=18\cos41^\circ\).

figure.alt: Triangle PQR is right at Q, angle P is 41 degrees, PR is 18, and PQ is a.
figure.caption: Read the sides from angle P.

content.prompt: Which is the exact value of \(PQ\)?
content.hint: From angle P, PQ is adjacent and PR is the hypotenuse. Solve \(\cos(41^\circ)=a/18\).

figure.alt: Triangle PQR is right at Q, angle P is 41 degrees, PR is 18, and PQ is a.
figure.caption: Read the sides from angle P.

blocks.html:
Another unit can describe the same angle

Radians measure angles with a half-turn equal to π. Since 180°=π radians, you can convert when the problem uses a different unit.

Degrees to radians

Multiply by π/180. For example, \(150\cdot\pi/180=5\pi/6\). Keep π for an exact answer.

Match the typed number to its unit

sin(30) in Degrees and sin(π/6) in Radians both give 1/2. Switching modes without changing the typed number does not convert that number to the other unit.

content.prompt: Which setup correctly evaluates the sine of a \(30^\circ\) angle?
choices: Type \(\sin(30)\) while Desmos remains in its default Radians mode.
Use Degrees mode and type \(\sin(30)\), or use Radians mode and type \(\sin(\pi/6)\).
Use Degrees mode and type \(\sin(\pi/6)\) for the same angle.
Angle mode does not affect the values that trig functions return.
content.hint: Either keep 30 as degrees or convert it to the equivalent radian measure \(\pi/6\).
content.explanation: Both matching setups produce the exact value \(1/2\). The entry and selected angle mode must describe the same angle.

blocks.html:
Matching angles keep the same trig ratios

Similar right triangles have equal corresponding angles. Their side lengths scale together, so each ratio stays the same. You can use a corresponding angle in the triangle containing the side you need.

content.prompt: Every side of a right triangle is doubled to create a similar triangle. What happens to the tangent of a corresponding acute angle?
choices: It is doubled, growing along with the two doubled side lengths.
It is cut in half, since the ratio now involves larger sides.
It stays the same because both opposite and adjacent are doubled.
It becomes \(90^\circ\), matching the enlarged right angle.
content.explanation: The scale factor cancels from the ratio, so tangent stays the same.

shared_prompt.title: Similar triangles ABC and DEF
shared_prompt.html: Right triangles \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) are similar, with \(A\leftrightarrow D\), \(B\leftrightarrow E\), and \(C\leftrightarrow F\). Also, \(\angle C=\angle F=90^\circ\), \(\angle A=38^\circ\), \(AC=10\), and \(DF=25\). Find \(EF\).

blocks.html:
Use the corresponding angle directly

Here A↔D, so angle D is 38°. In the larger triangle, EF is opposite and DF=25 is adjacent. Use \(\tan38^\circ=EF/25\), giving \(EF=25\tan38^\circ\).

figure.alt: Two similar right triangles are shown separately, not to scale. ABC is right at C, angle A is 38 degrees, and AC is 10. DEF is right at F, angle D is marked, DF is 25, and EF is unknown.
figure.caption: Diagrams not drawn to scale. Use the given correspondence A ↔ D.

content.prompt: Which is the simplified exact value of \(EF\)?
content.solution:
One route solves the small triangle and scales: \(BC=10\tan(38^\circ)\), and the scale factor to \(\triangle DEF\) is \(25/10\), so \(EF=(10\tan(38^\circ))(25/10)=25\tan(38^\circ)\).
The other route transfers the corresponding angle: \(A\leftrightarrow D\) gives \(\angle D=38^\circ\), and in \(\triangle DEF\), \(EF\) is opposite with \(DF=25\) adjacent, so \(\tan(38^\circ)=EF/25\) and \(EF=25\tan(38^\circ)\).
Both routes simplify to the same exact expression.
So the answer is choice B, \(25\tan(38^\circ)\).
content.hint: Simplify \((10\tan(38^\circ))(25/10)\), or use tangent directly in triangle DEF.
content.explanation: Both methods give the exact result \(EF=25\tan(38^\circ)\).

figure.alt: Two similar right triangles are shown separately, not to scale. ABC is right at C, angle A is 38 degrees, and AC is 10. DEF is right at F, angle D is marked, DF is 25, and EF is unknown.
figure.caption: Diagrams not drawn to scale. Use the given correspondence A ↔ D.

blocks.html:
Return to the two triangles

Try the opening question again. Choose the angle and side roles yourself, then find the requested exact length.

shared_prompt.title: Similar triangles JKL and MNP
shared_prompt.html:
Right triangles \(JKL\) and \(MNP\) are similar, with \(J\leftrightarrow M\), \(K\leftrightarrow N\), and \(L\leftrightarrow P\). Angles \(L\) and \(P\) are right angles. Also, \(\angle J=52^\circ\), \(JL=7\), and \(MP=20\).

Find the exact length of \(NP\).

content.prompt: Which is the exact length of \(NP\)?
content.hint: Use corresponding angles to find the acute angle in the triangle containing NP. Label opposite and adjacent from that angle, then choose the matching trig ratio.
content.explanation: \(\tan(52^\circ)=NP/20\), so the exact length is \(NP=20\tan(52^\circ)\). The trig-and-scale route simplifies to the same expression.
content.solution: \(\tan(52^\circ)=NP/20\), so the exact length is \(NP=20\tan(52^\circ)\). The trig-and-scale route simplifies to the same expression.

figure.alt: Two similar right triangles are shown separately, not to scale. JKL is right at L, angle J is 52 degrees, and JL is 7. MNP is right at P, angle M is marked, MP is 20, and NP is unknown.
figure.caption: Diagrams not drawn to scale. Use the given correspondence J ↔ M.

content.prompt: What makes a right-triangle trig setup reliable?
choices: Place the vertices, label sides from the right angle, choose a ratio, and match calculator mode to angle units.
Place the vertices, label sides from the chosen angle, choose a ratio, and keep calculator mode in Radians.
Place the vertices, label sides from the chosen angle, choose a ratio, and match calculator mode to angle units.
Place the vertices, label sides from the chosen angle, reverse the ratio, and match calculator mode to angle units.
content.explanation: The right angle fixes the hypotenuse; the chosen acute angle fixes the other side roles. Then the relevant pair selects the ratio.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: In right triangle \(DEF\), the measure of angle \(F\) is \(90^\circ\), \(DF=9\), and \(EF=12\). What is the value of \(\tan D\)?
content.explanation: From \(\angle D\), the opposite side is \(EF=12\) and the adjacent side is \(DF=9\), so \(\tan D=\frac{12}{9}=\frac{4}{3}\). \(\frac{3}{4}\) labels the sides from the wrong angle, and the ratios with \(5\) use the hypotenuse \(15\), which tangent never does.

figure.alt: Triangle DEF is right at F, DF is 9, EF is 12, and angle D is marked without a numerical measure.

content.prompt: Which expression gives the exact length of \(RT\)?

shared_prompt.title: Triangle RST
shared_prompt.html:
In right triangle \(RST\), \(\angle S=90^\circ\), \(\angle R=32^\circ\), and \(RS=14\).

Which expression gives the exact length of \(RT\)?

figure.alt: Triangle RST is right at S. Angle R is 32 degrees, side RS is labeled 14, and side RT is labeled with a question mark. No side is labeled with its trigonometric role.

content.explanation: From angle R, RS is adjacent and RT is the hypotenuse. Thus \(\cos(32^\circ)=14/RT\), so \(RT=14/\cos(32^\circ)\). Multiplying by cosine would make the requested hypotenuse shorter than the known leg. The sine choices treat the given leg as opposite angle R.
